### D1 - Answered: G1 — "generally similar behaviour, sensibly attainable."

*Date:* 2026-10-23

*Area:* Project process
*Status:* decided

**Answered: G1 — "generally similar behaviour, sensibly attainable."** Own deterministic engine; numbers exact where the dat is exact, tolerance-banded where behaviour is only observable through play. **G2 rejected** (after asking the owner directly what it would cost): no oracle here can show a per-tick trajectory, the original runs on x87 with 80-bit intermediates, and bit-exactness would mean transliterating machine code rather than writing an engine. **G1+ was considered and not adopted** — no per-subsystem exactness budget is committed. Owner's words: "I want generally similar behaviour, but sensibly attainable". The 13 saves validate constants and outcomes, not trajectories (`docs/archive/research/oracle.md`); the binary is 32-bit x86 with heavy x87 use (crude census: ~69k x87 escape bytes vs ~26k SSE `mov*` in `.text`), so exact-match work would not be *engine* work. Reaching for G2 also has a legal cost: a bit-exact clone is a derivative work, not interoperability. Exactness where it is cheap and free (dat values, fixed-point per-tick displacement, our own replay hashes); tolerances for behaviour, written down in §6.1. A subsystem may still be matched more tightly later as an optional experiment, but that is not part of the goal.

### D7 - TDD is mandatory

*Date:* 2026-10-23

*Area:* Project process
*Status:* decided

**TDD is mandatory.** No production code without a failing test first. The failing run must be recorded in the session before the implementation exists. Scope: engine crates + shipped tooling; throwaway analysis probes in `build/tools/` are exempt. Coverage is behaviour-based with **no percentage gate**. Project owner's requirement. A recorded failure is the only thing that distinguishes TDD from tests-after, which pass immediately and therefore prove nothing. A coverage % can be raised without testing a behaviour. Code found without a prior failing test is **deleted**, not retro-fitted. Every cycle report names the test and shows the command that saw it fail. Full rules: SPEC §11.


### D14 - Keep Ruage on HD 5

*Date:* 2026-10-23

*Area:* Project process
*Status:* amended

**Keep Ruage on HD 5.7 under G1; borrow narrowly; watch the field.** Concretely: (1) target HD, because it is frozen and a G1 engine's only asset is "the numbers are right today"; (2) adopt `librematch/genie`'s **format crates** only (D13) — never their engine core, because a nine-day-old repo with one author is a bus factor, and a narrow interface stays replaceable; (3) rebuild the step-6 backlog from the game's own subsystem split, as seen in their module list (§7.1); (4) offer HD-specific findings upstream (5.7 task lists, type-102 tech trees, the two decimal grains) so the relationship is two-way; (5) review prior art periodically and record what changed. Owner accepted the recommendation. The user's intuition that DE would be "too ambitious" is right about *bit-exactness* and wrong about the version: under G1, DE is a data target, not a mountain — what makes it costly is that it patches, so the target and the oracle both move. HD is frozen, which is worth more than the extra civs. No engine relicense; no dependency on their engine; a standing review of the field. A pivot to DE, or to linking a GPL reader at runtime (which would end D6), needs a new decision — not drift.

#### Amendment 1 (bank held two sections under one id)

The weekly watch (Monday 09:00 UTC) now leads with **SFTtech/openage** rather than treating the field
evenly, because it is the one project that has already paid the costs we are about to pay: a
from-scratch AoE2 engine with its own asset pipeline.

Four specific things to learn there, in order of usefulness to us:

1. **Their asset pipeline (D18).** How the install's SLP/DRS graphics are converted into openage's
   own formats, and how palettes, player colour, frame anchors and animation timing are handled.
   This is our asset-pack layer, and it is the difference between "graphics replaceable" being a
   schema and being a rewrite.
2. **Their engine/content split** - the *nyan* data format - against D17. Where is their boundary
   better than ours, and where does it force engine changes that ours avoids?
3. **Their determinism and networking posture, as a contrast and not a model.** openage's time
   subsystem is a wall-clock event queue with a 50 ms update cap, not a fixed tick (recorded under
   U12). Our tick loop is not negotiable, so this is the one place where being similar would be a
   mistake.
4. **Effect and tech modelling**, against what is pinned (kind 102 disables a tech, kind 4 adds an
   attribute, kind 5 multiplies) and what is not (U16's ambiguous `a` field, U17's negative packed
   attack).

**Licence rule, unchanged and not negotiable:** openage and the genie tooling are GPL-3.0. Reading
for ideas is fine; no code enters `crates/`, which is MIT/Apache. "It was only a small function" is
the sentence that creates the problem, and the watch is asked to flag anything that looks like it.

Still watched at lower priority: `librematch/genie` (format readers, exact-DE target - D13),
`SiegeEngineers/genie-rs` (dat modelling; check whether U15's `create_time` and U17's negative
packed values are now modelled there), and any new deterministic-simulation writeups.

The watch checks against our open questions rather than in the abstract: it is asked to name any
U-number a source now answers, and to say "nothing changed" when nothing did.

*Date:* 2026-10-23

*Area:* Project process
*Status:* decided

**Step-5 scope, decided: hand-authored map, scripted opponent, grid A* pathing.** The map is a 64×64 authored in `config/` (forests, berries, gold, two town centres) — not an `.rms` and not a `.scx`. The opponent is a fixed command list on a tick schedule, which doubles as our replay format. Pathing is A* on the static grid with the weights already in `movement.toml`. `.rms` (122 scripts), `.scx` (49 scenarios) and `.per` AI (74 scripts) are **future work, explicitly out of the slice** — each is a language or format implementation, not a slice feature. Owner's decisions on the three blockers. Each "future" item was priced: an RMS interpreter is a language implementation, `.per` likewise, and `.scx` needs a binary reader — none of them makes a villager gather wood. The slice's job is to prove the loop, not the content pipeline. Step 5 is headless, one civ (D3), British vs British (D13 terminology: our own map, our own opponent). Adding any of the three future sources is a new decision, not a refactor.


### D17 - Four layers, and only one of them is about Age of Empires

*Date:* 2026-10-25

*Area:* Project process
*Status:* decided

**Decided 2026-10-25.** The engine must be able to ship a game that is not Age of Empires II,
without being rewritten.

| layer | owns | may know about AoE2? |
|---|---|---|
| **engine** (`crates/`) | fixed-point determinism, tick loop, commands and replays, pathing, entity model, damage arithmetic, effect verbs | **no** — it knows *kinds* of things, never particular ones |
| **content pack** (`config/`, our schema) | resources, units, buildings, techs, effects, map, scenario — in our vocabulary | carries AoE2's *values* today; nothing about them is typed into the engine |
| **importer** (tooling repo, D12) | dat → content pack, plus the dat's semantics (packed attack, class ids, effect kinds) | **all of the AoE2 knowledge lives here** |
| **asset pack** | entity + state → sprite reference | today points at the install's graphics; later at ours |

The rule that follows: **any number or id that means something only because of AoE2 stays outside
`crates/`**. Pinning "kind 5 multiplies" and "attack is packed `class * 256 + amount`" is importer
work; the engine receives "add 1 to attack class 4".

Consequences already visible in the code:

- ~~`ResourceKind` is a fixed enum and stockpiles are `[[u32; ResourceKind::COUNT]; 2]` — four
  resources and two players in the *type*.~~ **Paid down 2026-10-26** (`docs/archive/research/plan-resource-deletion.md`):
  resources are content (`config/resources.toml`), a node carries a column, costs name their
  resource by reference id *or* by name, and the stockpile's width is the engine's `MAX_RESOURCES`
  with the pack's count checked at load. Proven by `a_content_pack_with_our_own_resources_loads_and_spends`.
  The player count was already data by D20.
- `script.rs` names `109` and `12`; the scenario format should name roles from the content pack.
  (**Still open**: the resource half of this is done - a step names a resource and the pack resolves
  it - but building and training still quote dat ids.)
- `Attribute::from_id` knowing 0/1/8/9 is fine *in the importer*, not in the engine.


### D18 - Target shape: A now, B-capable; assets swappable from the start

*Date:* 2026-10-25

*Area:* Project process
*Status:* decided

**Decided 2026-10-25.** The owner's words: keep the vibe and dynamics; start with the original
graphics, tech trees and stats; be ready to replace the graphics; move towards our own content as far
as the cost allows.

- **(a) now.** Reference content is the dat's numbers and the install's art. That is what makes the
  work verifiable: every mechanic has a known-good value to compare against.
- **(b) scheduled, not blocked.** Own resources, own tech tree, own stats — the engine must not need
  a change to accept them. That is what D17 buys.
- **(c) not planned.** Divergent rules (new resource set, ages replaced) would still be content, and
  the same schema should carry them; nothing is designed against that hope.

**Graphics readiness is a data question before it is a rendering question.** The dat carries a sprite
table — `slp_id`, `layer`, `force_player_color`, `color_table`, `num_deltas`, `bounding_box`,
`sound_id` — with animation deltas and player-colour flags, so an entity → sprite binding can be
**generated** by the importer rather than hand-authored. Two consequences:

1. the engine addresses visuals by a *content id*, never by a file name, so a replacement pack is a
   different table with the same shape;
2. sprite geometry the simulation needs (radius, footprint) is already in the unit table, so
   **swapping art cannot change gameplay** — which is the test to write when the first renderer
   lands.

**Not yet done, deliberately:** there is no renderer. The headless run is the harness, and a renderer
is a large piece of work that buys nothing until the simulation is worth watching. "Ready for
replacement" is therefore written as a schema and a boundary, not as a graphics engine.

**Verified / not verified.** The sprite fields above are read from `GenieDatParser`'s model at
`VER 5.7.2`. The unit → sprite *link* and how the install stores the numbered graphic resources
(DRS, and whether `slp_id` indexes it directly) are **not** checked yet — that is the first task of
the asset-pack work, not an assumption to build on.

### D86 - REA runs on this container; the Windows box is a target, not an analyst (2026-10-31)

*Date:* 2026-10-31

*Area:* Project process
*Status:* decided

The owner asked whether a Windows Hermes running REA could act as a slave delivering findings here. Measured
first, then decided; the numbers, versions and install traps are in `docs/archive/research/re-toolchain.md`.

1. **REA is an MCP tool server, not an agent**, and its Windows support is an experimental read-only boundary:
   27 Ghidra inventory/memory/function operations on native PE, x64-first, 32-bit PE admission only on its
   `main` branch, and a transport that is authenticated IPv4 loopback with a Job Object - deliberately not
   reachable from another host.
2. **The target is a 32-bit i386 PE** (`AoK HD.exe`, 7,521,280 bytes, PE timestamp 2018-08-22), which is the
   one cell that boundary admits worst, while Ghidra on Linux decompiles it with no restriction at all.
3. **So the analyser runs here**, beside the engine and the dat; the Windows machine keeps the job `oracle.md`
   gave it - run the game, produce save files. If a Windows agent is ever added for live-process work, A2A is
   the transport, and its output is artifacts plus provenance, never a mechanic asserted from a machine this
   one cannot re-derive it from.

Nothing in `crates/` changes for this: it is a toolchain decision, not an engine one.


### D87 - How ruage is compared to the original: a register ruled by reading, closed by recorded AI-vs-AI games (2026-11-01)

*Date:* 2026-11-01

*Area:* Project process
*Status:* decided

The owner's question was whether the disassembly can give the **complete** behavioural difference between ruage and
`AoK HD.exe`, "to rule one", with functional gaps deferred. The answer, written down rather than carried in a conversation
(`docs/archive/research/behaviour-diff.md`), is that completeness is not computable - 15,766 unnamed procedures with no PDB names, no
completion criterion for "have we found every rule", and code that is not behaviour. What replaces it is a **register**:
one row per rule ruage implements, each ruled *same / different / unknown-static / needs-oracle* with the original's address
and our file:line. The count is honest and small: **1 of 12 ruled today**.

The owner then stated the other half of the method: **two AIs playing each other, the match recorded, with captures taken as
it runs** - "then we have a multitude of the data points". That is the oracle D2 already defined, pointed at a match nobody
has to play by hand.

Consequences, and they are what future sessions should act on:

1. **Static reading proposes, the game disposes.** Rows that are local arithmetic can be ruled from the binary alone; rows
   about tick order, pathing tie-breaks, decay and the age-up boundary cannot, and are marked `needs-oracle` rather than
   guessed.
2. **The mode is Random Map, not Death Match** - RM exercises the economy and age ramp that our timings differ on, and DM's
   AI is unrepresentative because it never earns anything. DM is kept for the combat rows later.
3. **Saves matter more than screenshots.** A screenshot closes no register row; two saves five minutes apart close the decay
   row outright. The capture set is therefore record + periodic saves + event screenshots.
4. **Nothing install-derived is committed** (D8/D22) - recordings and saves stay out of the repo; the finding and a SHA-256
   go in.
5. **Settled 2026-11-01, by the owner: both player slots can be set to AI.** The farm is a plain all-AI match, with no
   workaround and no passive human slot - which is what makes it a data source rather than a chore.


### D90a - The workspace denies hash iteration and a bare `#[allow]` (2026-11-01) (bank id D90)

*Area:* Project process
*Status:* live (bank numbering collision — see C13; bank status was amended)

Borrowed in shape from `librematch/genie`'s lint set, adopted on the owner's "adopt adoptable". Determinism rule 3 says
no collection the sim walks is a hash map, and **nothing enforces it**: this workspace has no `[workspace.lints]` section
at all, so the rule rests on review. `clippy::iter_over_hash_type` is available on this toolchain and free today because
`crates/` holds no `HashMap`.

Adopt: a `[workspace.lints.clippy]` section denying `iter_over_hash_type`, and the same section denying a new `#[allow]`
that carries no reason (`allow_attributes_without_reason`). D88 is why this is not a style question - the moment fights
are ordered, the iteration order *is* the rule.

**How to verify a lint config, since a lint cannot be unit-tested from inside the thing it lints:** introduce the
violation on purpose once (a `HashMap` walk in a scratch test), watch the build fail, remove it, and record the failing
output in the commit or the day's review. `crates/sim/tests/no_float.rs` is the precedent for pinning a rule that would
otherwise be a comment.

### D90b - A missile whose launcher died does no damage (2026-11-01) (bank id D90)

*Area:* Project process
*Status:* live (bank numbering collision — see C13; bank status was amended)

The owner's second combat rule, verbatim: **"For projectiles also cause zero damage once launcher died in original game. If
trebuchet goes missile and dies, missile causes 0 damage."**

This closes the gap D88 deliberately left open - D88 ordered melee blows and left arrows in flight alone, with the note that
ordering arrows was "a second decision the owner has not given". He has given it, and the answer is not "order the arrows"
but **"the arrow lands and is worth nothing"**.

Implemented as: the landing checks its shooter, and if the launcher is gone (swept on death) or at/below zero (killed earlier
in the same tick) the landing resolves nothing - no damage, no blast, no retaliation, no carcass. The arrow still flies and
still disappears; only its blow is void.

Consequences worth naming: a razed tower's volley already in the air hits nothing (same rule, no special case); a dead
hunter's arrow leaves no carcass; and the rule is invisible in the acceptance match (its hash did not move), which means the
case does not arise there rather than that the rule does nothing.

### D139 - The second review's sim block: seven fixes, and what the block actually was

*Date:* 2026-11-07

*Area:* Project process
*Status:* decided

*2026-11-07. The 63 findings filed against `crates/sim/src/`. Read against the current tree; seven fixed here.*

1. **The block is not the engine core.** 19 findings against `script.rs`, 14 `bin/batch.rs`, 12 `bin/headless.rs`, 9
   `metrics.rs`, 9 `path.rs` - the script layer, the two tools, the metrics watcher and the path module. `lib.rs`, where
   `step`, the mover and the economy live, was not in it.
2. **A class-level correction, third time tonight:** `f64 as i64`/`as u32` **saturate** (Rust 1.45+). Of the five findings
   built on casts, three are wrong about the mechanism ("wrap", "panic in debug", "`Infinity as i64` is `i64::MIN`"), and one
   is right for the opposite reason - the range check never fired because the cast *succeeded*, clamped.
3. **Fixed (7), each with a test watched failing first except the binary rename:**
   - `path.rs:127` - `line_clear` refused a line whose **start** tile is occupied, while `find_path` allows a blocked start
     on purpose; every unit on a node paid a full A* for a line it could see.
   - `path.rs:127` - the same closure tested containment *and* `blocked()`, which already answers `true` off-map: a second
     bounds check per tile.
   - `path.rs:33` - `Walk::from_map` now asserts `terrain.len() == width * height` in debug builds; `Map` is public and
     fixtures build it directly.
   - `script.rs:1162` - `has_unit` matched one unit id, so `has_unit = "militia"` went false at the man-at-arms upgrade.
     `is_family` now.
   - `script.rs:583` - an attack step naming `militia` refused with *"no unit militia"* after the upgrade. `is_family` now.
   - `script.rs:271/287/307` - `Runner::new` accepted `tick_rate_hz = 0`, and accepted `at_seconds = 1e300` as 9.2e18 ticks
     through the saturating cast, making its own "does not fit in a tick" message unreachable. Both refuse now.
   - `bin/batch.rs` - the binary was documented as **`ruage-batch`** in its own USAGE, in `SPEC.md`, in `next-step.md` and
     in `config/acceptance.toml`, and cargo built it as **`batch`**: every documented invocation named a file that did not
     exist. The file is renamed `src/bin/ruage-batch.rs`, and a live `--seeds 7` run prints `#f328ebc8d4d34b78`.
4. **Refuted (6)**: saturating occupant counters (deliberate, documented); `octile`'s `as u32` (max ~3,610 for u16 tiles);
   `index`'s `None` (it *is* the bounds guard); `metrics`' multiply (seven orders inside `i64`); `nth_villager` exact id (one
   villager role, no upgrade in 5.7); and the two cast-mechanism claims above.
5. **Deferred (26 with reasons, 24 cheap and queued).** The queue's head, and the reason it is the head:
   - `script.rs:1533/1541` - **the enemy selectors can aim at a Gaia town centre or a foundation**; `enemy_town_center` does
     not filter `player != 0` and neither filters `construction.is_none()`.
   - `script.rs:1103` - a rule condition naming a role or resource the pack lacks makes the rule silently **never fire**,
     with nothing in `rule_refusals` - the D137 defect, one layer up.
   - `batch.rs:192`, `headless.rs:181` - a `duration_seconds` of 1e300 is a 9.2e18-iteration loop; `tick_at` applies.
   - `headless.rs:300` - `players=` prints the highest player id, not the count.
6. **Acceptance unmoved**: `f328ebc8d4d34b78`, 141 entities, 188 repaths, 187 made-room, 574 refusals, **11.47 / 11.51 s**
   over two idle runs. The 16.97 s figure I reported earlier was a run whose compile overlapped the suite; withdrawn.

5. **Public API is unchanged**, and the near-miss is recorded: a text promotion appended `pub(crate) ` to signatures that
   were already `pub` (`max_scale_for`, `MAX_PLAYERS`), producing `pub pub(crate)`. Rule: promote only a signature that
   starts with four spaces and `fn `.
6. **The proof is the hash per move**: `f328ebc8d4d34b78`, 141 entities, 188 repaths, 187 made-room, identical after each of
   the twelve. 728 passed / 0 failed / 19 ignored; clippy and fmt clean.


### D152 - Priority order: functionality, UI, graphics, AI, music - and what "functionality" is missing

*Date:* 2026-11-07

*Area:* Project process
*Status:* superseded

*2026-11-07. The owner: "Q9, I don't care about comparison and AI now. That would be addressed later. Pathfinding and
general functionality matter for now. I think best order of priority is: 1 general functionality, 2 ui, 3 graphics, 4 AI,
5 music."*

1. **The order is recorded and governs**: general functionality first, then UI, then graphics, then AI (D151 is a plan that
   waits), then music. No AI work until 1-3 are where he wants them.
2. **Pathfinding is measured, not assumed.** `find_path_avoiding` costs **8.9 us** corner to corner on a 64x64 map (D143,
   two flat `Vec<u32>`), applies the **both-corners** rule for diagonals, refuses a line whose start tile is occupied
   (D139), and the world **smooths** the route by jumping to the furthest node `line_clear_avoiding` reaches (`lib.rs`
   `plan_path`). A short-range pathfinder module (`src/short.rs`) already exists for the local case the original game uses.
   The review's "a sealed map expands the whole grid" is true and costs **~9 us**, not a stall - so it is not the next
   thing to fix, and saying otherwise would be inventing work.
3. **The functionality gaps are the documented ones**, each with its decision: **no gates** (D54 - a wall blocks its owner
   too, because pathing is one grid), **no unit pushing** (D52 - overlap is possible and a unit already sharing a tile is
   never moved aside), **fog without occlusion** (D50 - sight is a disc, not a line through terrain), and **victory rules**
   beyond the seat (which the owner has now explicitly deprioritised: a working economy and a filling military queue are the
   pass condition, not victory).
4. **Order within 1**: **gates first** (a wall the owner can pass is the difference between a wall and an obstacle, and it is
   a pathing question, which is what he named), then **unit pushing** (D52), then **fog occlusion** (D50).
5. **UI and graphics already have a foothold**, so they are not greenfield: `crates/view` has the bar, panel, minimap,
   widgets, layout and a frame buffer (U1-U3, SPEC v1.68-1.70), and there is **no renderer** by choice (D18) - graphics
   begins at sprites (SLP) and the entity+state -> sprite binding that the dat's sprite table can generate.


### D164 - `cargo run` starts the window

*Date:* 2026-11-08

*Area:* Project process
*Status:* decided

*2026-11-08. The owner typed `cargo run --release` to get the debug output and got *"could not determine which binary to run"*.*

1. `crates/view/Cargo.toml` gains **`default-run = "window"`**, so `cargo run --release -p ruage-view` starts the game; the `frame`

2. **Why it was not left alone**: a second binary in a package silently re-opens this, and the first command anyone types to start the game

### D193 - a test asserts the rule and quotes the measurement

*Area:* Project process
*Status:* decided

**What it says.** A test states the **relation** (`distance_to_tile(worker, tile) <= radius`) and may quote the measurement that
motivated it in its failure message. It does not assert the measurement. A measurement stays in a test only when the measurement *is*
the claim - a save-game fixture saying what the owner's file holds.

**Why, measured.** When the standoff moved from a 1.156-tile ring to the tile's border (D192), **eleven gather tests went red at once**,
every one of them asserting the number rather than the rule. The engine was *more* correct and the suite said it was broken, and rewrite
blame lands on whichever side is cheaper to change - which is never the rule. Recorded in SPEC §11 with both forms side by side.


### D195 - the next step is one step

*Date:* 2026-11-12

*Area:* Project process
*Status:* decided

**What it says.** `docs/next-step.md` is capped at **16,384 bytes**, must start with `# OPEN`, and `tools/next_step.py --split` moves
everything after the first block to `docs/history/next-step-<date>.md`. Enforced by `make check` and the pre-commit hook.

**Why, measured.** The owner's rule is "compact first: persist state to files so a fresh session resumes without the conversation". By
2026-11-12 that file was **350,038 bytes** - twenty times the largest source file - and this session read it at 101 KB and growing
before it could start. One run moved **348,807 bytes** out and left **1,230**.


### D203 - a rule asked for twice goes into the tree, and a question the owner must answer arrives after the evidence

*Date:* 2026-11-13

*Area:* Project process
*Status:* decided

**What it says.** Three standing instructions the owner gave on 2026-11-13, written down because a rule that lives in a
conversation does not reach the next thread:

1. **Every step is bracketed by a compact and an adversarial review.** The compact's first half is the feature's *prior
   implementation* - where it lives (`file:line`), which tests pin it, what it measures today - because a plan written
   over an unnamed implementation cannot say what it is changing. The review comes after the change, covers performance
   **and** stability, and carries a measured number. `AGENTS.md`'s four-step routine is that rule; its step 1 now says so.
2. **A decision the owner must make is the last step, not the first.** The order is: the original game first (run it,
   watch it, read its own data, read the binary), then the adjacent open-source projects and published sources
   (`docs/prior-art.md`, the wiki, the manual), and only then the question - which carries what each attempt found,
   including the attempt that found nothing.
3. **The question does not expire.** It goes in the reply with the turn ended, and it is recorded as a `U<n>` row in the
   U-register before that, so a reboot at 04:00, a new thread or a week's silence cannot lose it. A `clarify` form is for
   a choice that blocks the current step; `agent.clarify_timeout` is now `0`, so a form that is open cannot expire
   unanswered mid-conversation - but a form holds the turn, so it is not where a decision question goes.

**Why.** The owner asked for it in these words: *"I always want to compact prior implementation of feature and then
adversarial review on performance and stability after that. When my decision is needed, I always want original game to be
checked how it deals with the problem, if no solution is found then I want other OSS projects and other sources in the web
to be checked and then provided with the question which never timeouts with information gathered."* Each of the three has
already failed once here: a review was skipped twice before `tools/review_check.py` existed, a `clarify` form came back
unreadable and expired unanswered (`references/docs-and-decision-index.md`), and a question asked inside a thread was gone
with the thread.

**The enforcement, and what it does not cover.** Compact: `tools/next_step.py --check` refuses a `next-step.md` over
16 KB or not headed by one open step, and `.githooks/pre-commit` runs it. Review: `tools/review_check.py` refuses a
commit that changes `crates/`, `config/`, `tools/`, `Age2HD/` or `build/` without a staged note holding a measured
`## Performance` and a `## Stability`; the hook runs that too. Question: `tools/decisions.py --check` refuses an open
`U<n>` with no area in `docs/decision-areas.toml`, and this entry files itself (`D203 = "Project process"`). **Nothing
here stops `--no-verify`**, and no script can tell whether a review is honest - only a reader can. The gate's claim is
the narrow one: omission has to be deliberate.

**Commits us to.** A `clarify` form is never where a decision question goes; a question worth the owner's attention is
worth the evidence hunt before it, and a hunt that found nothing is part of the question rather than a reason to skip it.


### D208 - the order of work is a checked tree, and the mechanics we defer are deferred by seam

*Date:* 2026-11-14

*Area:* Project process
*Status:* decided

**Owner, 2026-11-14**, six answers to the questions `docs/archive/research/dependency-tree.md` §12 carried: *(1)* the target is **a correct
engine**, not a playable product first; *(2)* **one civ** until the data debts close; *(3)* monks, trade, naval and relics
are **not in v1, but the architecture must be ready for them**; *(4)* publishing is **B** - the engine and its tooling
public, the spec and the mechanics internal; *(5)* the binary register's **row 2 now, then the oracle**, because rows 3-12
are `needs-oracle`; *(6)* "the enemy is eliminated inside 40 minutes" is **not a requirement**.

**What it settles, and what it replaces.** Every slice in this project has carried its own plan, and the plans were written
in whatever order the last session happened to work in - so a slice would be started and then found to depend on something
unbuilt. The owner's request was a tree of the items, their status and the order, and this is it: `docs/archive/research/dependency-tree.md`,
**64 items** in five groups - foundations, the simulation, **the debts**, the missing mechanics, the product - with the
edges, seven phases and a gate per phase. The debts are the finding: **fourteen places where a row marked done is hollow**,
each proved by a probe that can fail (attribute 1 is `Range` where the game means line of sight; nothing reads construction
rate 195; `DisableTech` is parsed and never consulted; no farm reseed queue; a Horse Collar farm holds 325 against the
game's 250).

**What it builds.** One document, one check and one rule. `tools/plan_check.py` (**eight checks, ten tests**) refuses the
ways a status table rots: an id defined twice or referred to and never defined, an open item that no phase names, a
`DONE-ish` row whose hole is unnamed, a status outside the legend, a citation whose file does not exist or whose line is
past the end, and a `U`/`D` id the corpora do not have. It runs in `make check`. The **seams** are the answer to the owner's
third answer without building the mechanics: R1 a body has a domain and ground has a surface; R2 an order that is an
ability; R3 a roll is its own seeded stream; R4 victory is a content table; R5 a price is state. Each is proved by a fixture
*pack*, never by the mechanic, and none puts a game's word in `crates/` (D17).

**What it costs.** Measured, five runs: **266 ms** over the document (32,577 bytes, 64 items, 104 citations). The first
version took **3,304 ms** because its file index walked `target/`; pruning the walk made it 12× faster. Nothing here is in
the tick - the tool is Python and is never linked into the engine. On first run the check found **six genuine misses in the
document it was written for** (M4-M7 and T8/T13 unscheduled, S11's hole named by an `M` while only a `T` was accepted), and
two defects in the tool itself were found by mutating it rather than by reading it.

**What it does not settle.** A green check says the document is *consistent*, never that a status is *true*; a row that
lies passes. That is what §11's probes and the adversarial review are for. Four stale claims were found while writing the
tree and are recorded there rather than quietly fixed in their own files: D152 still lists gates and unit pushing as
missing (D154/D204 shipped them), `civs.rs`'s header says the team bonus is unapplied (`research.rs:221` applies it),
`window.rs` says there is no input or HUD, and SPEC v1.153's "the standoffs still use the ring" was superseded by D192.

**Amended 2026-11-14, after a survey of the original and its neighbours.** The owner asked whether the original game and
the published engines hold items the tree was missing, and they do: the install's own strings and its 104 `.per` AI files,
plus `librematch/genie`'s systems list and `Zaydme/openaok`'s feature list, added **M11-M25** (waypoint queues, follow and
guard, the town bell, facing and the animation clock, player diplomacy, tribute, treaty, the market's prices, trade carts
and cogs, victory modes beyond conquest, scenario triggers, random map generation, the `.per` interpreter, the network
layer, and chat/taunts/flares/cheats) and **T15-T17**. Two of those correct the tree rather than extend it: the random
protocol is **eleven streams reseeded from a frame seed every tick** (not "a roll is its own stream", which was R3's
weaker form) and there is a **turn** (only one player's unit AIs run fully), so R3 was rewritten and T15/T16 sit in
Phase 3. Six candidates were **refused as later-build features** — pastures, the mule cart, Empire Wars, `Wait_Solidify`,
genie's passive-ability task kinds and `fmath` — because their names are zero hits in `AoK HD.exe` or they are DE
content, and they are recorded in `docs/archive/research/dependency-tree.md` §5b so the next session does not port them.

**Basis.** The owner's six answers, quoted above; the tree's own probes (`grep -rn '\b195\b' crates`, `DisableTech` in
`crates/sim`, `reseed`, `crates/data/src/techs.rs:96`); the importer's name table,
`ruage-tools/genconfig/records.py:125`. Review: `docs/reviews/2026-11-14-plan-check.md` and
`docs/reviews/2026-11-14-dependency-tree.md`.


### D219 - civ and team bonuses are a seam with a written design, not v1 work

*Date:* 2026-11-15

*Area:* Project process
*Status:* decided

**The ruling (the owner, 2026-11-15).** *"Team bonuses and other civilisation bonuses can wait. Let's just have the design ready
for it to be implemented in the future."*

**Why it is the right call, measured.** Of the **31** civs with a team-bonus effect, the modifiers name `line_of_sight` 24
times, `gather_rate` 17, **`other:101` 16**, `population` 12, `attack` 11, **`other:23` 8**, **`other:100` 7**, `minimum_range` 3
and `range` 2. So **23 of the ~100 team-bonus modifiers land on an attribute nothing in the engine reads**, and `other:23`
another eight - "apply team bonuses" is not one switch, it is a table two thirds of which is still unnamed. Two of the bonuses
also carry a **kind-102 row** (a bonus that *bars* a tech), which the current mental model does not cover, and kinds **3** and
**6** appear in this data with no reader anywhere.

**What was written instead of code.** `docs/archive/research/civ-bonuses.md`, and a sixth seam in `docs/archive/research/dependency-tree.md` §7b (**R6**): one
resolved `BonusTable` per player - resources, attributes keyed by the enum rather than by string, barred techs, barred units,
granted units - rebuilt on the two events that can change it (a tech landing, the civ being set), with the five consumers that
walk those three tables today becoming five readers of one table. The proof is stated as a test: a fixture **pack** with a
synthetic civ whose team bonus increments resource 36 and names `line_of_sight`, and the existing consumers answering 265 on a
farm and a wider tower sight **with no new engine word**.

**What this decision does *not* do.** It invents no numbers, names no attribute, and implements nothing: the five walks stay
exactly as they are, and the two team-bonus resource rows that matter today (36 for the farm line) keep working through
`farm_food_bonus` as D215 left them. R6 is placed in Phase 3b beside R1-R5 - after the determinism work, before civ breadth,
because breadth is what multiplies the call sites it replaces.

**Basis.** A probe over `config/gamedata/civs.toml` and `effects.toml` (counts in `docs/archive/research/civ-bonuses.md`); the five consumer
sites (`barred_by`, `civ_barred_unit`, `modifiers_for`, `farm_food_bonus`, `construction_rate`); D214's finding that the
attribute *string* is the interface, which is what makes a resolved table worth writing before breadth.


### D224 - the parked set was audited, not trusted: three of the four "live defects" are not defects

*Date:* 2026-11-15

*Area:* Project process
*Status:* decided

**What it says.** The four items the gap report called live were checked by **running** them (`cargo test -- --include-ignored`)
rather than by reading their `#[ignore]` sentences. Three were not defects at all, and the fourth was a fixture measuring the
wrong geometry:

- **`depletion.rs`** - no test in the file carries `#[ignore]`. Both rules (a standing tree blocks its tile, a chopped one leaves
  no obstacle) pass, and always did; the *module doc* claimed the first was "parked with `#[ignore]`". Corrected.
- **`retarget.rs` (D98a)** - green: the forager finishes the bush, walks to the adjacent farm, and the food column rises. The
  parked sentence named node 103 as the wrong choice and never said which change was missing. Un-parked; the audit did **not**
  bisect which change fixed it, and the note says so instead of claiming one.
- **`carrier_no_pushing.rs` (D204)** - green: the crowd carrying home is not pushed. Un-parked.
- **`gather_contact.rs` (D181)** - **the engine was right and the fixture's yardstick was wrong.** "Touching" is measured against
  the node's **tile square** - `distance_to_tile <= body + a fiftieth of a tile`, i.e. 0.22 for a villager of 0.2 - so a body
  whose circle is against the tile's **corner** sits `sqrt(2) x 0.72` = **0.93** from the tile's centre. D181's measurement,
  "took while 0.92 tiles from the bush", is that corner contact to the hundredth, judged by a **radial** yardstick. The fixture
  now measures the tile (`ruage_sim::tiles::distance_to_tile`), passes, and **bites**: widen the gate to any adjacent tile and it
  reports the take at **0.47** tiles off the tile. No production line changed.

A sweep of every parked test that does not take minutes followed, all green: `boom_probe` 1, `collision_probe` 2 (378 s),
`settle_probe` 1, `sheep_probe` 1, `short_probe` 1, `pathing` 6, `movement_worth` 2 (349 s), `acceptance_economy` 3 (94 s). The
`perf` and `stability` probes are measurement-only and were not part of it.

**Why this matters more than the four items.** The tree had been carrying a **false work queue**: a session reading
`docs/next-step.md` would have spent four slices rediscovering that three defects are gone and one was a measurement error, and
each of those slices would have "fixed" working code. `#[ignore]` is a *claim about the past*; only running it says anything
about the present.

**What it costs.** Nothing in the simulation: one test file corrected, three un-parked. What it buys is the queue below the
queue - the real debts (`T7`, `T14`, `T2`, `T6`, `T8`, `T11`-`T16`, and the `M`/`P` rows) are now the only live items, and
`docs/next-step.md` says so.

**Basis.** The sweep (`d224-parked.txt` in the scratch dir), the two mutations on `gather_contact`, and the gate.
Review: `docs/reviews/2026-11-15-d224-parked-audit.md`.


### D235 - the world writes itself down, and a load is proved by ticking the same (2026-11-16, P1a)

*Date:* 2026-11-16

*Area:* Project process
*Status:* decided

**What P1 needs and what this is.** `P1` (dependency-tree, Phase 4) is `World::from_state` plus a tool-side converter, in the
**B shape** the owner ruled on 2026-11-14: the converter lives in `tools/`, so no reader of the game's save file ever enters
`crates/`. The converter has nothing to convert *to* until the engine can write and read its own state, and **that** half is
what landed here. The RE half - walking the save's sections 2-4 for civs, stockpiles and the object list, none of which is
read yet (`docs/archive/research/save-format.md`) - is not started and is not pretended to be.

**The shape: `serde` on `World` itself, not a `WorldState` mirror.** A mirror is a second list of the world's 95-odd fields,
and the second list is the one that goes stale - this project has paid for exactly that shape twice (the farm line and the
builder speed, D234). With a derive, a field added to `World` is in the file the next time the crate compiles, and the
round-trip fixture fails if the load does not restore it. What is **not** in the file: the pack's tables and rules
(`techs`, `effects`, `civs`, `resources`, `units`, `economy`, `damage_rules`, `command_apply`) - those are the game's, not the
match's, so a state carries the pack's **identity** and a load against another pack is refused by `PackMismatch`, naming both.
The two derived caches (`bonus_tables`, `sight_modifiers`) are not written either: they are rebuilt on load, which is what
makes a forgotten rebuild a test failure rather than a file that looks complete.

**MessagePack, and why not JSON.** The state is keyed by numbers in a dozen places (`BTreeMap<EntityId, Route>`,
`researched: BTreeMap<u8, BTreeSet<u32>>`). JSON insists map keys are strings and refuses to read them back, so JSON meant
either a `#[serde(with)]` helper on every map - the second list again - or MessagePack, which keeps the **names** (it is
self-describing) and reads integer keys. MessagePack won.

**Three failures the fixture found while this was being built, all mine.** (1) `units` and `economy` are pack data and were
skipped on the way out; not putting them back left the loaded world with no unit table, so every stat read as absent and the
two worlds parted company at the first step. (2) The obvious way to restore the pack - call `load_civs` - **re-assigns** each
player's civ from `economy.start.civs`, and the start state belongs to the match, not the pack, so a loaded world was given a
different civ from the one its state named; the load now installs the civ *table* and rebuilds the two caches instead.
(3) Serde's `skip` needs a `Default`, and `command_apply` has no sensible one - the pack's answer is not available while
parsing - so it has a documented placeholder that `from_state` overwrites before the world is returned.

**One hole closed on the way.** `civs.toml` has been in the pack's hash since D19, but `ContentPack` did not expose it: a
consumer had to open the file again, which is how a load and a handshake can disagree about what the pack is. It is a field
of `ContentPack` now.

**What it costs.** Nothing on the tick: no line of the tick's code changed, and the acceptance hash is
`cb1f6a83a119a2a3` on both sides at 24,000 ticks. The write and the read are off the tick path - measured below in the review -
and the state is written only when something asks for it.

**Basis.** `crates/sim/src/world/snapshot.rs` (`Written`/`Read`, `World::state`, `World::from_state`), the `serde` derives on
`World` and its 24 field types, `crates/data/src/pack.rs` (`civs`), `crates/sim/tests/state.rs` (three fixtures: round trip
identical at 0 and 100 ticks, a cut state refused, another pack refused by name). Review:
`docs/reviews/2026-11-16-d235-state.md`.


### D240 - A decision is retired, never deleted - and a supersede link is read from one side only (owner, 2026-11-16)

*Date:* 2026-11-16

*Area:* Project process
*Status:* decided

The owner: *"Can you clean superseded/obsolete decisions?"* The corpus is 245 decisions and 544 KB, and a session reading it
cannot tell a live rule from one that a later decision killed unless it also reads the killer.

**Deletion is not available, and that is checked rather than remembered.** `tools/decisions.py`'s `check_shrink` compares the
corpus against `HEAD` and refuses a commit that lost an id - added after 2026-11-12, when the corpus fell from 187 decisions to
one and `--check` stayed green because the area table was truncated with it. So a rule that is dead **keeps its id and its body**
and gains a pointer at its head; nothing else is touched, because the body is the evidence for whatever replaced it.

**What "clean" meant here, in three parts.**

1. **A duplicate id was split.** Two full sections were headed **D200**: the attempt built on `d189-owner-blind` and parked on a
   measurement, and the rule that actually shipped. The parser read the first as the decision and the second as an amendment, so
   the *index* showed the parked one's title. The parked section is now **D200a** ("superseded by D200, then partly withdrawn by
   D239"), and `D200` is the shipped rule - which is what every citation in `crates/` and `docs/` means by it.
2. **The decisions D239 takes half of carry a withdrawal marker**, at the head, naming exactly what went: D204 (the next-node
   re-target and the idle-body nudge), D238 (step 1, "a seated body must not be past"), D127 and D135 (the cap of two), D200a
   (the nudge, the slide and the give-way).
3. **The supersede links were being computed in the wrong direction, and two decisions were falsely dead.** The parser read
   *"the clause is superseded by D10"* as "D10 is superseded by this decision", so **D10 - the live scale rule - was rendered
   `superseded`**, and **D208** was marked dead by D192 for writing *"SPEC v1.153's sentence was superseded by D192"*, where the
   subject is a document and the speaker is a bystander. Only the **forward** form is parsed now (*"X supersedes D9's clause"*),
   which is also this file's own convention: a reversal adds a row, and the new row says what it replaces. Pinned by
   `tools/test_decisions.py::SupersedeDirection`.

**What this leaves open, named rather than implied:** a decision whose rule is gone from the tree but which **nothing supersedes**
- a slice reverted by measurement (D141, D236) - has no marker class yet, and `check` cannot see it. Recognising that class needs a
probe per decision (does the symbol it names still exist), which is a tool of its own and is not built.

**Basis.** `tools/decisions.py` (`check_shrink`, `SUPERSEDES`), `tools/test_decisions.py`, `docs/decision-areas.toml`,
`docs/archive/decisions-2026-11-24.md` (D200a, D204, D238, D127, D135). Review: `docs/reviews/2026-11-16-d240-retirement.md`.


### D246 - the reply is short, the code is simple, and both say why where the reader needs it (2026-11-16)

*Date:* 2026-11-16

*Area:* Project process
*Status:* decided

**What it says.** Two standing instructions from the owner:

1. **The reply is quick to read.** Answer first, then the evidence; short paragraphs and short lists; no preamble, no
   restating the request, no "great question". A number, a path or a quoted command instead of a mood.
2. **The code is written for the next reader.** The simple thing that works, not the general thing that might - add the
   abstraction when the third caller appears. Readability and maintainability are requirements, not polish, and comments
   explain **what a thing is for and why it is shaped that way** (the invariant, the trap, the measurement behind a
   constant), never what the line does.

Both are in `AGENTS.md`, in the file every session in this tree loads before it writes anything.

**Why.** The owner's words, 2026-11-16: *"Provide easy to understand quick to read text output, avoid AI slop and wall of
text"* and *"focus on simplicity, readability of the code and maintainability, avoid overengineering, most of the cases
have simple solution. put in the code comments providing good explanation of functionality"*. Both failures cost him the
same thing - the time spent separating the answer from the prose around it, or reading a general mechanism where a
function would do.

**What it does not mean.** *Short* is not thin: a rule still carries its measurement and a review still names what was
attacked. *Simple* is not naive: the fixed-point, determinism and layering rules stay exactly as strict; what goes is the
abstraction with one implementation and one caller, and the clever line that needs a paragraph to defend.

**Commits us to.** A reply that opens with the answer and stops when the answer is done; comments that carry purpose and
provenance rather than narration; and naming the case where the simple version is not enough instead of building the
framework in advance.


### D249 - the conformance set ignores nothing: a red test is a rule we do not keep (2026-11-16)

*Date:* 2026-11-16

*Area:* Project process
*Status:* decided

**What it says.** The owner, the day D247 landed: *"None of the conformance tests is to be ignored. If it collides with HD
functionality, please tell me and let me decide with provided findings from the game."* So:

- **No `#[ignore]` anywhere in `crates/conformance`.** A rule the game keeps and we do not is a test that **fails**, named in
  the reply with its source. An ignored test is a decision nobody re-reads, and this set exists to stop exactly that.
- **The set is its own workspace** (`crates/conformance/Cargo.toml` carries `[workspace]`, the root lists it in `exclude`), so
  a red conformance test can never turn the repository's gate red: `cargo test --workspace` does not build it, and
  `make conformance` does. That is what lets it be honest without holding the tree hostage.
- **A collision is the owner's ruling, not ours** - filed as **U25** with the game's evidence, our answer, and the cost of
  each option, so it cannot expire with the conversation.

**State of the set at this commit: 28 green, 5 red.** The red five are three rules of the game we do not keep (U25 a, b, c)
and one defect of ours, measured twice (U25 d).

**The defect, and why it is not fixed.** `nearest_reachable` answers **one step from the start**, not the tile nearest the
click: its queue is popped best-first by distance to the click, but every tile it pushes is already free, so the first pop is
a neighbour of the start. From (1,1) toward (10,10) on empty ground it answers (2,2); a click into a wood six tiles away is
answered beside the walker's feet. Its own doc comment and D134 claim the opposite, and `click_into_the_woods.rs` misses it by
spawning the villager **one tile** from the wood, where the bug's answer satisfies "within one tile of the block".

The fix was written and measured, and **reverted** because it costs the match:

| build | entities | players | hash | repaths |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| HEAD `45b5bd2` | **155** | **1** (won) | `8cf433ad4e0205f4` | 497 |
| HEAD + the sweep | **125** | 2 (not won) | `0f0a37dc86bf1002` | 451 |

Both runs are the same worktree, same generated data, seed 7, 48,000 ticks, release, differing in **one file**. The cause is
measured, not guessed: the acceptance script issues exactly **two** unreachable clicks, both `(26,13) -> (25,17)`, and the
sweep sends the villager six tiles to `(25,19)` where the bug sent him one step - a diverted villager at 1,303 s is enough to
lose the win. Cost of the corrected call: **143 us** on a 64x64 map and **1.1-3.2 ms** on a 200x200 (the box was shared while
measuring), paid only on the fallback path - not the reason it was reverted; the match was.

So the fix is a fork for the owner, not a defect to land quietly: adopt it and retune `config/acceptance.toml` (the script is
ours; the game has no one-step answer), or keep the one-step behaviour and say so, in which case the two tests assert our
answer and cite D134's rule as the one we do not meet.

**Commits us to.** Never adding an `#[ignore]` to this set; adding a rule only with its source; and presenting a collision as
a decision with its evidence rather than as a parked test.


### D278 - The acceptance floor is the win, not an entity count (owner, 2026-11-18)

*Date:* 2026-11-18

*Area:* Project process
*Status:* decided

**The ruling, in his words.** Asked to choose between the queue's `entities >= 155` floor and the match's own outcome: *"restate
it to the win"*.

**What the floor was, and why it inverts.** D242 and D250 gated slices on **`entities >= 155` and `repaths` near 380**. The
numbers say what is wrong with it: `main` at 2026-11-18 reads **131 entities and `players=1`** - a *won* match - while the build
that read **154 entities never resolved**, and the D250 build read **137 and won at 2,381 s**. An entity count is a proxy for
"a live match", and it inverts at exactly the moment that matters: when a side loses its base, its units stop being trained and
the count **falls**. So the floor punished winning.

**The gate, from now on - three numbers, none of them a proxy:**

1. **The match resolves** at or before 48,000 ticks: `players=1` (one side eliminated) or an explicit draw. A run that ends with
   `players=2` and live refusals saying the economy cannot reach its next age is a **failure** regardless of its entity count.
2. **The economy is alive**: the acceptance script's last refusal must not be a resource wall at the end of the run - `"not
   enough food: 500 needed, 195 in the bank"` from 2,387 s is the signature of a stalled economy, and it is now a named failure
   rather than a curiosity.
3. **Nothing that was green goes red**: the suite is the rule set, and the acceptance is not allowed to buy a win by breaking a
   fixture.

**Where the win cannot be read, the floor goes back to its old job**: a *pure movement probe* (a crowd, a corridor, a march) has
no match to win, and its own fixture is the gate. The floor applied to the acceptance match only, and it was always being quoted
about the acceptance match.

**What this changes in practice.** The two parked branches re-read as: `d276-no-slide` **fails** (players=2, food wall at 2,387 s)
and `d276-prefix-only` **passes** (players=1, unchanged) - the same verdicts as before, now for a stated reason rather than a
number that happened to agree.

**Basis.** Measured in this tree: `main` 131 entities / `players=1` / `b5292af5a6072d57`; the D250 build 137 / won at 2,381 s; the
control 154 / never resolves; `d276-no-slide` 153 / `players=2` with the food wall from 2,387 s. Register: D242's and D250's
floors are superseded as gates, and their measurements stand.

**Commits us to.** Every slice reports **the win, the food wall if any, and the entity count** - the count as information, never
as the gate - and a slice that wins with fewer entities is a slice that won.


### D319 - The conformance gate was dead, and one divergence row was stale

*Area:* Project process
*Status:* decided

**The owner asked whether conformance tests are still skipped. The answer was worse than yes: the crate did not compile, so none of its
rows had run since D306.**

```
error[E0061]: this method takes 5 arguments but 4 arguments were supplied
   --> tests/budget.rs:63:38, 76:38, 95:37
```

`Ground::search_reporting` gained a `reach` argument in D306 and `budget.rs` still passed four. The crate is its own workspace (D247) so
that a **red** rule can never block a commit - the right call - but nothing in `make check` so much as **built** it, so a signature change
in `crates/sim` silently took the whole set out of service. Its own comment, "no test in it is `#[ignore]`d", was false too.

**Landed.** `budget.rs` passes `reach = 0` (the tile search's own value, which is what those three rows are about). The one `#[ignore]`d
divergence - *"the radius lives in the step, not in the planner"* - was made false by D303-D306 and is now a live conformance row,
`the_search_grows_obstacles_by_the_bodys_radius`: a body a tile wide is planned **through** a one-tile gap (tangency is a passage, the
owner's trebuchet measurement) and a body 1.2 tiles wide is **not**. Both halves were watched: with `reach = 0` substituted for the wide
body the row fails with *"a body 1.2 tiles wide was planned through a one-tile gap"*. The hierarchy row's doc no longer says "not ported
yet" - it landed in D296-D302. **And `make check` now compiles the conformance tests** (`conformance-build`, `--no-run`) without running
them, so D247's hazard stays shut while the staleness cannot recur.

**Measured.** Conformance set **21 tests, 21 pass, 0 ignored** (was: does not compile; before that 19/1 with two rows parked). The build
step costs ~9 s cold, under a second warm. The main workspace is untouched: **928 / 0 / 21** stands.

**Still ignored, named rather than hidden**: the main workspace keeps **21** `#[ignore]`s - **19 instruments** (perf and measurement
probes that print, plus the two four-hour determinism runs) and **2 real gaps**, `a_passer_by_does_not_move_the_seated_gatherers` (D238)
and `a_stopped_friend_is_not_walked_through` (R1b). Neither is a fixture the owner asked for; both are ours, with their causes written
down.

### D333 - Two parity rows closed by measurement, and P3 narrowed to one number

*Area:* Project process
*Status:* decided

**P9 was already done**: its two halves - arrival "beside a held goal" (D200) and the crowd ring point (D271) - went with D292 and D289 at the
owner's own instruction, and `grep` finds neither in the tree. The row said "forks forfeited" for work that had already been cut; third time
this register has pointed the next step at ground already covered.

**P6 is nominal, measured**: the ground's per-tile `occupants` count only differs from the game's per-object boxes when an object is **narrower
than its tile**, and every object this content carries is exactly a tile wide - all four resource kinds have `radius = 0.5` (a tile's
half-extent) and blocking buildings take dat radii of 1.0, 1.5 or 2.0. The row now says what would reopen it.

**P3 is blocked on one float.** `FUN_00840830` read in full: the overlap test is an **inclusive AABB** (`min <= other_max && other_min <=
max`, so touching counts, the `<=` the register quoted), applied to a box that is **shrunk on all four sides** by `+0x268` when the flag at
`+0x266` is set. That inset is what makes D306 possible - a half-tile body still fits a one-tile gap because the query box is inset - so the
inclusive test cannot land without it, and the inset's formula is not in the corpus. **Our `object_depth > 0` is the same rule from the other
side**: refusing penetration into a box is refusing touching of a box inset by a hair.

**What is left of "remove all deviations" is not code**: P3 needs one number, P12 needs the per-edge mask read, and P11's polygon pathfinder is
a project with no hull code in the tree. Everything else is done, nominal, or - P10 - deliberately kept, because a reproducible random source
is what makes the acceptance hash possible.

**Measured**: no code change - acceptance `e248486298910e28` (127 entities, 1,727 re-paths, 10.2 s), suite **933 / 0 / 19**, conformance
**21 / 0 / 0**.


### D352 - Conformance is a line on every ruling, and the divergence register is the one list of what we do differently

*Date:* 2026-11-22

*Area:* Project process
*Status:* decided

**The owner's instruction, 2026-11-22, and the frustration behind it, verbatim**: *"Could you please FFS purge our rulings which
are not conformant with original game, decomp or online sources once and for all? It is bloody touring [tiring] having to repeat
over and over that the original game and decomp are to be followed only to find out they were not..."*

**What the bank actually looked like, measured rather than assumed.** 238 decision rows; **3** talked about the game while
pointing at no source (all three honest: D151 quotes the owner and `docs/archive/research/ai-extraction.md`, D166 is a rendering choice and says
so, D184 says its accident needs a model we do not have). So the *provenance* of the bank is not the disease. The disease is the
other thing the tool cannot see: **a row that cites the right address and reads it wrong** - D348's "the margin is zero", D341's
`has_route && moved` standing in for `isMoving`, my own D349 misreading of `FUN_007f9d80`'s `&&` this evening, D267 reading
`func_002699A0` as group placement only. Each was corrected by **re-reading the expression**, and each cost a slice first.

**What this row establishes, in three parts.**

1. **A conformance line on a ruling.** Any row may carry
   `**Conformance**: GAME - <pointer>` / `OURS - <why>` / `UNVERIFIED - <what would settle it>`, and a row that talks about the
   game carries one or a source pointer. `tools/conformance_audit.py` lists the ones that do neither; it is a **burn-down list,
   not a gate**, because a wrong gate teaches a fake line (`0%` taught exactly that, D209).
2. **One register of divergences**: `docs/divergence-register.md`. Two verdicts only - **DEFECT** (read, ours, with the source
   and the step that closes it) and **OURS** (deliberate, with what the game does instead). Eleven defects and five ours as of
   today, every one with its pointer. **A claim about the game that is in neither section is a claim waiting for a source**, and
   it goes in `next-step.md` as a read, not into code.
3. **The supersession order, restated because it is the sentence he keeps having to repeat**: the original game (binary, dat,
   install) > the decomp > the neighbour projects > published sources > **our own rulings, including his** > our convenience. A
   ruling of ours that contradicts a reading is not "a decision we follow" - it is a **DEFECT** row, and the reading wins.

**What changes in behaviour: nothing.** This row is a mechanism and a register. The purge it orders is the eleven DEFECT rows,
one slice each, and the first is D351 (branch `d351-reseat`) with the three plan ports behind it.


### D355 - the bank becomes a page: 341 rulings in 8k tokens, and the fixture column that names the lies

*Date:* 2026-11-22

*Area:* Project process
*Status:* decided

**Conformance**: OURS (process). The owner, 2026-11-22: *"Is too many decisions causing problems with context being filled and
starting to forget?"* - and the answer is yes, but not the way the question guessed.

`docs/archive/decisions-2026-11-24.md` is **832,998 characters** (~210k tokens), larger than a context window: it cannot be loaded, so a session can
only grep it, and a ruling it does not already suspect exists is a ruling it will not apply. That is not hypothetical - a session
on this date wrote **D349-D354** while **D150 already held the owner's pile rule**, and then built a fixture that could not tell
the rule from its absence. `docs/decision-areas.toml` - the index built for exactly this (D166) - named **2** decisions and left
**49** (D283-D332, the whole pathfinding run) with no area at all, and `docs/reviews/` held **309** notes with nothing listing
them.

**So:** `tools/decision_index.py` writes `docs/decision-index.md` - **341 rows, one line each** (claim, verdict, source, fixture,
area, supersession) in **34k characters / ~8k tokens**, plus the three lists that matter: **claims the game with no source** (5),
**names no fixture** (**247**, the "believed implemented" list), **superseded** (3). `tools/review_index.py` writes
`docs/reviews/INDEX.md`: 309 notes, one line each. Both are generated, committed, and neither is a gate.

**The convention that makes the fixture column worth having**: a ruling that rests on a test names it (`Fixture: <name>` in the
row, or a `tests/<name>.rs` path). A row that names none is the work list - 247 rows long tonight, and emptied one measurement at
a time, never by inventing a name.

**Also in this slice**: D351's row carried onto this branch read-only (the register cites it, and a citation of a row that exists
only on `d351-reseat` was a dangling reference `tools/decisions.py` reported); 51 rows given areas; `decisions-check` back to
**0**; `AGENTS.md` opening with the two indexes and the convention.

**Fixture**: `tools/test_decision_index.py`, 6 cases over a sample bank (title-as-claim, verdict from the `Conformance` line
only, a declared fixture beating a filename, supersession read both ways, area scored not first-match).
